The Human Connectome Project (HCP) faces the challenging task of bringing multiple magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) modalities together in a common automated preprocessing framework across a large cohort of subjects. We describe the minimal preprocessing pipelines for structural, functional, and diffusion MRI that were developed by the HCP to accomplish many low level tasks, including spatial artifact/distortion removal, surface generation, cross-modal registration, and alignment to standard space. These pipelines are specially designed to capitalize on the high quality data offered by the HCP. The final standard space makes use of a recently introduced CIFTI file format and the associated grayordinate spatial coordinate system. Here, we provide the minimum image acquisition requirements for the HCP minimal preprocessing pipelines and additional advice for investigators interested in replicating the HCP's acquisition protocols or using these pipelines. results.title: Negligible effect of brain MRI data preprocessing for tumor segmentation - ScienceDirect
results.content:
Title: Negligible effect of brain MRI data preprocessing for tumor segmentation - ScienceDirect
# Negligible effect of brain MRI data preprocessing for tumor segmentation. Although a preprocessing pipeline standardizes image appearance, its influence on the quality of image segmentation and on other downstream tasks in deep neural networks has never been rigorously studied. For instance, the set of preprocessing steps for brain MRI images has remained relatively stable and has been reproduced across the majority of papers on the topic from the early 2010s until now. Here we challenge the conventional pipelines for MRI image processing and question their necessity for accurate prediction with regard to new advanced deep learning machinery. While the motivation behind applying these steps is clearly to standardize image appearance and remove different sources of domain shift [8], these steps are computationally costly and their utility for deep-learning segmentation lacks investigation. In this study we analyze the most popular preprocessing steps for brain MRI data and measure their influence on deep-learning based tumor segmentation tasks. First, we numerically estimate the effect of 7 common preprocessing steps: resampling images to equal size, inter-subject atlas registration, resampling voxels to equal size, bias-field correction, image denoising, histogram matching, skull stripping; with state-of-the-art deep learning architectures that are both convolutional and attention-based. Third, we suggest a minimal preprocessing pipeline for multi-sequence brain MRI studies, leading to the highest brain tumor segmentation quality and consisting of two steps3: Resampling images to an equal voxel size and Skull stripping. Image preprocessing is a de-facto standard first step in almost all deep learning pipelines for medical image analysis [10]. We extent the Results section with Conclusion and our recommendations on MRI images preprocessing for deep learning-based tumor segmentation. We perform a rigorous ablation study of the most conventional preprocessing steps used in the analysis of brain MRI images, including atlas registration, resampling fixed voxel of image size, histogram matching, bias-field correction, denoising and skull stripping. ### Brain extraction on MRI scans in presence of diffuse glioma: Multi-institutional performance evaluation of deep learning methods and robust modality-agnostic training. ### A fully automatic procedure for brain tumor segmentation from multi-spectral MRI records using ensemble learning and atlas-based data enhancement. ### Brain tumor segmentation based on deep learning and an attention mechanism using MRI multi-modalities brain images.
